name: Armenian SSR
info: The Soviet republic of Armenia, with its capital at Yerevan, created by the Sovietisation of the First Republic in 1920, which grew from an agricultural hinterland into an industrial centre and became independent in 1991.

facts.founder: The Armenian Bolsheviks with the 11th Red Army; the Revkom led by Sarkis Kasyan and Avis Nurijanyan took power in December 1920
facts.successor: The Republic of Armenia, independent on the dissolution of the Soviet Union (26 December 1991)

t: Soviet Armenia was established on 29 November 1920 with the Sovietisation of the First Republic, and the treaties of 1921 left Kars, Ardahan and Surmalu, with Ani and Mount Ararat, to Turkey and Nagorno-Karabakh and Nakhichevan to Soviet Azerbaijan.
In its 71 years the republic changed from a largely agricultural hinterland into an industrial centre, and its population grew from about 880,000 in 1926 to 3.3 million in 1989.
The Karabakh movement of 1988 led to the Declaration of Independence of 23 August 1990, and Armenia became an independent state when the Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991.
dyk: According to Khrushchev's memoirs, when Turkey objected to Mount Ararat on Soviet Armenia's emblem, the Kremlin asked why Turkey had a half moon on its flag, since the moon did not belong to Turkey either; Turkey dropped the issue.
ev: On 29 November Soviet Armenia is established as the 11th Red Army enters and the government of the First Republic hands power to the Bolsheviks
The Armenians rise against the Revkom in February; the Treaties of Moscow and Kars leave Kars, Ardahan and Surmalu to Turkey, and in July Nagorno-Karabakh is given to Soviet Azerbaijan
Armenia joins Georgia and Azerbaijan in the Transcaucasian SFSR, one of the four founding republics of the Soviet Union
First Secretary Aghasi Khanjian is killed by Lavrentiy Beria in Tiflis on 9 July, beginning the Great Purge in Armenia; the TSFSR is dissolved and Armenia becomes a union republic
About 150,000 Armenians of the diaspora, mostly survivors and descendants of the genocide, settle in Soviet Armenia
On 24 April thousands demonstrate in Yerevan on the 50th anniversary of the Armenian genocide; the memorial at Tsitsernakaberd follows in 1967
The Supreme Soviet of the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast votes on 20 February to unite with Armenia, starting the Karabakh movement; a devastating earthquake strikes the republic
Armenia confirms its independence by referendum on 21 September, and the Armenian SSR ceases to exist with the dissolution of the Soviet Union on 26 December

sections.foundation:
Eastern Armenia had been part of the Russian Empire since the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828, and Armenian Marxism remained a minority movement until 1917. In May 1918 the First Republic of Armenia emerged, governed by the Armenian Revolutionary Federation and burdened by refugees from the 1915 genocide. After the Red Army took Azerbaijan in April 1920, the Armenian Bolsheviks led an uprising at Alexandropol in May, which the government suppressed. In September Turkish forces invaded, and by the end of November the 11th Red Army had entered the republic. The Yerevan government sent Alexander Khatisian to negotiate with the Turks and appointed a team under General Drastamat Kanayan to hand power to the Bolsheviks.

Soviet Armenia was established on 29 November 1920. A pact of 2 December promised the pre-September borders and an amnesty for officials, but the Revkom of Sarkis Kasyan and Avis Nurijanyan, arriving with the Red Army, arrested Dashnak leaders. Its war communism meant, in the words of the Soviet Armenian historian Bagrat Borian, indiscriminate seizures and confiscations; requisitioning and the terror of the local Cheka led the Armenians, under former leaders of the First Republic, to revolt in February 1921 and briefly unseat the government in Yerevan, until the Red Army returned from Georgia to suppress the rising.
sections.socioeconomy:
In the early years 80% of the population worked the land. Under Stalin private farms were forcibly collectivised against peasant resistance, especially in Lori, Daralagiaz and Zangezur, and industrialisation from 1929 raised industrial output by 1935 to 650% of its 1928 level. The changes broke up the traditional peasant family and village and drove many into the towns; by 1991 about 80% of Armenians were town dwellers working in heavy industry, management and services. Under Khrushchev farms were divided, private plots allowed, and tobacco, vegetables, grapes and other fruit grown instead of grain alone; under Brezhnev tourism prospered, and the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, launched in 1976, supplied Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan, while pollution and corruption grew.

The population almost quadrupled, from about 880,000 in 1926 to 3.3 million in 1989, through natural growth and the arrival of genocide survivors and their descendants. After the Second World War about 150,000 Armenians from countries such as Cyprus, France, Greece, Iraq, Lebanon and Syria came between 1946 and 1948. They spoke Western Armenian, were received coldly by many, and thousands of them, suspected of Dashnak sympathies, were among those exiled to the Altai Krai in 1949. By the 1979 census over 99% of the republic's people considered Armenian their national language.
sections.military:
The republic had no forces of its own: its garrison was the Soviet Army's 7th Guards Combined Arms Army of the Transcaucasian Military District, with headquarters in Yerevan and motor rifle divisions at Kirovakan and Leninakan. Its early years were won by force. The Red Army suppressed the revolt of February 1921, and the anti-Soviet rebellion of Garegin Nzhdeh in mountainous Zangezur was defeated, its leaders driven across the Araks River into Iran on 15 July 1921.

The Wehrmacht never reached the South Caucasus, but Armenia supplied food, manpower and war material in the Great Patriotic War. An estimated 300,000 to 500,000 Armenians served, almost half of whom did not return. Over 60 Armenians became generals, Ivan Isakov an admiral, and Ivan Bagramyan, Hamazasp Babadzhanian and Sergei Khudyakov marshals of the Soviet Union; the aircraft designer Artem Mikoyan co-founded the MiG design bureau. On 7 June 1945 Vyacheslav Molotov told the Turkish ambassador that Kars, Ardahan, Artvin and Surmalu should be returned to the Soviet Union in the name of Armenia and Georgia, a claim backed by the Catholicos and every part of the diaspora, the Dashnaksutiun included. With the Cold War and the Truman Doctrine Turkey turned to the West, and the Soviet Union dropped the claim.
sections.governance:
The republic was governed by the Communist Party of Armenia, a branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union: the First Secretary was its administrative head, the Chairman of the Council of Ministers headed the government, and the Supreme Soviet in Yerevan, elected for five years, was its legislature. From 1930 it was divided into up to 37 raions. In 1921 Lenin sent Alexander Miasnikian to replace the Revkom's methods with a moderate policy attuned to national feeling, and under korenizatsiya Armenian became the official language, illiterate citizens up to the age of 50 were sent to school, and the spelling was reformed.

Under Stalin the republic's leadership was destroyed. Beria's struggle with First Secretary Aghasi Khanjian ended with Khanjian's killing on 9 July 1936; Beria's men, Amatuni Amatuni and the NKVD chief Khachik Mughdusi, arrested 1,365 people in ten months, among them the writers Charents, Bakunts and Zabel Yesayan. After Sahak Ter-Gabrielyan's death in NKVD custody in August 1937, Stalin sent Georgy Malenkov and Anastas Mikoyan to purge the party; more than a thousand were arrested and Grigory Arutinov became party leader. Catholicos Khoren I was murdered in 1938 and the Catholicate of Ejmiatsin closed. In 1978 Armenians and Georgians defeated a proposal to remove their languages' official status.
sections.impact:
The NEP years brought a cultural revival under the formula 'national in form, socialist in content'. Alexander Tamanian began his city plan for Yerevan, an institute for culture and history opened at Ejmiatsin in 1921, the Yerevan Opera Theatre and a dramatic theatre were built, and Martiros Saryan, Yeghishe Charents, Avetik Isahakyan and others produced popular works of art and literature. Hamo Beknazarian directed the first Armenian feature film, Namus, in 1925, the first Kurdish film, Zare, in 1926, and the first Armenian sound film, Pepo, in 1935; the Kurdish newspaper Ria Taza was founded in 1930.

After Stalin's death Mikoyan urged the rehabilitation of Charents and Miasnikian, purge victims were rehabilitated, and the Stalin statue over Yerevan was pulled down in 1962 and replaced by Mother Armenia in 1967. The Matenadaran opened in 1959 to house the nationalised manuscripts of Ejmiatsin, the Arpa–Sevan tunnel was built to save Lake Sevan, and contacts with the diaspora revived. The genocide memorial at Tsitsernakaberd followed in 1967 and Rafayel Israyelian's memorial to the Battle of Sardarabad in 1968; Karen Demirchyan's government built the Yerevan Metro and Zvartnots International Airport. Soviet textbooks called the Caucasus, and Armenia in particular, the oldest civilisation on Soviet territory.
sections.decline:
The question of Nagorno-Karabakh, given to Azerbaijan in 1921, never went away: its Armenians appealed to Khrushchev in 1962, Anton Kochinyan asked Moscow in vain for unification in 1966, and the petitions went on through the 1970s. Under Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika the Supreme Soviet of the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast voted on 20 February 1988 to unite with Armenia. Demonstrations in Yerevan's Theater Square in support grew into the Karabakh movement. Violence against Armenians in Sumgait, ethnic rioting, the devastating earthquake of 1988, in which the shoddy apartment blocks of the Brezhnev years were the first to collapse, and a further pogrom in Baku turned Armenians against the Kremlin.

Moscow's indecision on Karabakh, the slow relief after the earthquake and the failing economy widened the gap between Yerevan and the centre. On 23 August 1990 the Supreme Soviet adopted the Declaration of Independence, naming the state the Republic of Armenia. Armenia boycotted the union-wide referendum of 17 March 1991 on preserving the Soviet Union, and after the failed coup in Moscow it confirmed its independence by referendum on 21 September 1991, with more than 99% in favour. With the Belovezha Accords and the dissolution of the Soviet Union on 26 December 1991 the Armenian SSR ceased to exist; its constitution of 1978 remained in force until July 1995.

summary: The Armenian SSR was created in 1920 when the Red Army and the Bolsheviks took over the First Republic of Armenia. Through collectivisation, the Great Purge, the Second World War and the return of genocide survivors it became an industrial republic of 3.3 million, and the Karabakh movement of 1988 led to its independence in 1991.
references: Ronald Grigor Suny, Looking toward Ararat: Armenia in Modern History (Indiana University Press, 1993)
Mary Kilbourne Matossian, The Impact of Soviet Policies in Armenia (E.J. Brill, 1962)
Razmik Panossian, The Armenians: From Kings And Priests to Merchants And Commissars (Columbia University Press, 2006)
Simon Payaslian, The History of Armenia: From the Origins to the Present (Palgrave Macmillan, 2007)
Christopher J. Walker, Armenia: The Survival of a Nation (St. Martin's Press, 1990)
Claire Mouradian, De Staline à Gorbatchev. Histoire d'une république soviétique (Ramsay, 1996)

pointDescs.1920: The 11th Red Army enters Armenia and Soviet Armenia is established on 29 November; the Revkom arrests Dashnak leaders.
pointDescs.1921: The February revolt against the Revkom is suppressed; Miasnikian brings the New Economic Policy, but the treaties of Moscow and Kars cost Kars, Ardahan and Surmalu, and Nagorno-Karabakh goes to Azerbaijan.
pointDescs.1922: Armenia joins the Transcaucasian SFSR, one of the four founding republics of the Soviet Union.
pointDescs.1929: Industrialisation begins, and Stalin's forced collectivisation meets peasant resistance in the mountains.
pointDescs.1935: Industrial output reaches 650% of its 1928 level; Pepo, the first Armenian sound film, is released.
pointDescs.1936: Khanjian is killed by Beria on 9 July and the Great Purge begins in Armenia; the TSFSR is dissolved and Armenia becomes a union republic.
pointDescs.1937: After Ter-Gabrielyan's death in NKVD custody, Malenkov and Mikoyan purge the party: more than a thousand are arrested and Arutinov takes over.
pointDescs.1941: The Soviet Union enters the Great Patriotic War; 300,000 to 500,000 Armenians serve, almost half of whom do not return.
pointDescs.1945: The war ends; Gevorg VI is elected Catholicos and allowed to reside at Ejmiatsin, and Molotov claims Kars and Ardahan from Turkey.
pointDescs.1948: About 150,000 repatriates from the diaspora have arrived since 1946; thousands are exiled to the Altai Krai in 1949.
pointDescs.1954: Mikoyan's speech in Yerevan on 11 March calls for the rehabilitation of Charents and Miasnikian, opening the Thaw in Armenia.
pointDescs.1959: The Matenadaran opens in Yerevan to house the manuscripts of Ejmiatsin; contacts with the diaspora revive.
pointDescs.1965: Thousands demonstrate in Yerevan on 24 April for the 50th anniversary of the genocide.
pointDescs.1967: The genocide memorial at Tsitsernakaberd is erected, and the statue of Mother Armenia replaces Stalin's over Yerevan.
pointDescs.1976: The Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant is launched, supplying Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan; tourism and industry grow under Brezhnev.
pointDescs.1979: Over 99% of the republic's people give Armenian as their national language in the census, after Armenians defeated a threat to its official status in 1978.
pointDescs.1988: The Karabakh movement fills the streets of Yerevan; the Sumgait violence and the earthquake follow, and Armenians turn against the Kremlin.
pointDescs.1990: On 23 August the Supreme Soviet adopts the Declaration of Independence of Armenia.
pointDescs.1991: Independence is confirmed by referendum on 21 September, and the Armenian SSR ends with the Soviet Union on 26 December.

notes: The saved article lists no works (its Bibliography and Further reading sections are empty), so references are [].
The article says demonstrations involved nearly one million Armenians 'by the beginning of 1988' though the movement began on 20 February 1988; the figure is left out.

The 2013 Gallup and 2017 Pew polls on the breakup of the Soviet Union are left out as present-day opinion. The changes of the republic's formal name (1936, 1937, 1940, 1966, 1989) are left out for length.
The 1935 agricultural index (132% of 1928) is left out; only the industrial figure is used. The strength curve's peak (1976) is a judgement on the Brezhnev-era economy, not a figure from the article.
The article's positive framing ('stabilization and security from hostile neighbors') is not repeated; the profile states the dated developments.
